I have spent many years looking at droplets. Their size, their shape, their position. But sometimes it is worth looking below the droplet. For many years I have followed the work of Pavel Levkin and his team at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) . What always impressed me is that they asked a different question. Not "How can we dispense better?" but "What if the surface becomes part of the experiment?" The answer is the Droplet Microarray. Instead of using physical walls, the surface itself keeps every droplet exactly where it belongs. Every droplet becomes its own tiny reaction chamber. This opens the door for applications like single-cell studies, high-throughput drug screening, organoid research or experiments with very limited patient material. Things that would quickly become expensive or impractical in larger volumes. As an engineer, I really like this way of thinking. Sometimes innovation is not about building a better machine.
